newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico exporters seen thriving despite firm peso.
newsitem.headline: Mexico exporters seen thriving despite firm peso.

text.p: Mexican industrialists may be alarmed because they can no longer rely on a weak peso to boost exports, but their earnings are still strong because of cheap labor costs, greater efficiency and a reviving domestic economy, analysts said.
"It's only natural that as a currency appreciates or stabilizes, exporters are the first to scream out," said Walter Molano, economic and financial research director at Swiss Bank Corp.

Exporters in Mexico actually benefited from a shock devaluation of the peso in December 1994. The currency's slide made them relatively immune to the domestic economy, which went into its worst recession in decades.

In recent months, however, exporters have expressed concern the peso may be overvalued, as domestic inflation has far outstripped the peso's slide against the dollar. Over the past 12 months, the peso has slid by about 3.8 percent whereas 12-month inflation is currently running at 20 percent.

That situation led Javier Prieto, president of the Northeast Foreign Trade Council, to declare on July 31 the peso's current valuation was a "big warning light" for exporters based in the northern industrial city of Monterrey.
Molano estimated the peso was fairly valued in terms of purchasing power parity but was still undervalued by 35 percent when deflated in terms of unit labor costs.
Kerry McHugh, industrial sector analyst with the Goldman Sachs brokerage, also stressed the advantage of cheap labor costs for Mexican conglomerates.

"A weak peso will help exporters, but big deal. Anyone can export that way," said Daniel Goldstein of ING-Barings, who added that many conglomerates had boosted internal efficiency through enhanced operating leverage.
"If they are still exporting, they do indeed have a comparative advantage," he said.
Industrial companies were also offsetting the effects of a stable peso by switching to the domestic market to reap the benefits of economic recovery, the analysts said.
Many of them pointed to steelmakers Hylsamex and Ahmsa as examples of that trend.
Alexander Anderson, research head at the Abaco brokerage, said conglomerates such as Grupo Carso, Alfa and Vitro VTR.MX produce a diversifed range of goods, allowing them to tap a domestic recovery.

Several analysts also noted a stronger peso actually proved to be an advantage when it came to paying off heavy dollar-denominated debt held by conglomerates. Furthermore, lower U.S. interest rates led to lower interest expense for Mexican conglomerates, they said.
The analysts said they did not expect the peso to stay at its current level, seeing a slide of 4 to 5 percent before the end of the year.
"They could possibly earn more from a five percent devaluation, but they cannot complain about the numbers they are posting," McHugh said.
